newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo securities watchdog pushes for more control.
newsitem.headline: Yugo securities watchdog pushes for more control.

text.p: Yugoslav securities watchdog body on Monday announced one of its first harsher measures to block the unofficial financial market and threatened to revoke licences to brokerages refusing to submit activity reports.
"By doing so, they refuse to reveal the full extent of their over-the-counter trading," the Yugoslav Securities Commission (YSC) Secretary Stoja Milosevic told Reuters.

According to Milosevic, at the end of August YSC named four brokerages -- Energobroker, Eki Broker, Cacak Broker and Preduzece Bankarski Platni Sistemi -- which had not presented their reports in time.
"They simply hide an increasing volume of trade in giro money -- trading surplus liquidity among banks -- and also hide high commission they charge for their service," Milosevic said.
Milosevic warned that not even a promissory note was used as a payment guarantee.
"Now we have decided -- either they oblige to our control or we shall revoke their licence," she added.

The Yugoslav financial market, roughly divided between the official bourse and the unofficial giro money market dominated by the mainly insolvent banks, has faced tightened liquidity since mid-September when the central bank launched the 10 percent reserve requirement.
The central bank's measure was aimed at imposing an even stricter control over inflation and the expanding money supply.
Since the reserve requirement was launched, commercial banks responded by neglecting the central bank bonds, which offer attractive interest rates and low investor risk.
Banks instead turned to the giro money market for fresh and short-term borrowings.

According to the Belgrade Stock Exchange report for the week ending October 4, the official bourse turnover fell about 32 percent to 25.39 million dinars ($5.027 million) while the unofficial giro money market volume rose by almost 90 percent to reach 42.57 million dinars.
YSC claims that giro money market is not controlled by any single institution.

Milosevic said banks devoted their surplus funds to "highly speculative market operations", instead of financing local companies, who face a chronic lack of working capital needed to kick start production.
"It is fine with us, but then they should instead become real investment banks and operate as such. If not, they will have to go to the bourse," Milosevic insisted.

But a market analyst said banks were simply trying to find money as soon as possible and cover their negative balances. "Otherwise they risk losing their licences," the analyst said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
